job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Wei Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm doing a master's in power systems at Northgate University, and I still live at home in Marlow with my parents and my little sister. My day is a bus ride with a thermos, lectures, then the lab where we model how a grid copes with too much solar. Mum is a ward nurse and Dad drives a city bus, and my grandparents sold their flat and set money aside for my studies, so I have no debt.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why the master's rather than a job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My bachelor's was a pass, nothing special, and my final project on a solar inverter controller worked, but only just. I figured a master's in power systems would open doors, because the grid needs people for the next thirty years. I use a chatbot now and then when my code won't compile, but I double-check everything it says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's about time people stopped panicking. At home Dad would nod and say he's seen cheaper buses called revolutionary before. Online I'd probably share a joke and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the plan I made last year still works: finish in June, apply to the grid operator and a couple of utilities, and start at a normal graduate salary. Plenty of firms hire near Marlow, and my family's money gives me a cushion of more than six months. I don't have much to be nervous about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chatbot only for boring things like formatting a report, and keep studying. I'd apply to about twelve utilities and engineering firms in the spring. I'd also ask my lab partner Jonas to do mock interviews with me, because I'm bad at talking about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A little guilty that I'm so lucky compared to other people on my course who have loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the grid work you want depend on AI at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Grid planning is physics and rules, and a lot of it is regulations a person has to sign. A chatbot helps me write a script faster, but it doesn't decide where a substation goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your sister Noor, who is thinking about a nursing degree like Mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister Noor to go for nursing, because a robot won't hold a patient's hand. Mum's hospital can't find enough nurses either. I'd also tell her to watch Mum's shifts first, so she knows what she's signing up for.

say: Good, it's about time people stopped **panicking** about it.
Dad would say he's seen cheaper buses called a revolution before.
think: My plan still works: finish in June and apply to **utilities** near Marlow.
I have over six months of **cushion**, so I'm not nervous.
do: Apply to about twelve **utilities** and engineering firms in the spring.
Practise **mock interviews** with my lab partner Jonas.
feel: Pretty **calm**, with a small dose of guilt about my luck.

Mentions guilt about classmates with loans, which keeps him humble about his luck.

steps.text: Apply to twelve utilities and engineering firms in spring
Do mock interviews with lab partner Jonas
Use the chatbot only for report formatting and scripts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for productivity if the gains are shared. Otherwise it's just fewer jobs for the same pay. I'd back stronger rules so firms can't cut graduate intake without telling anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the first tasks to go are the ones graduates do: running the load-flow scripts, writing the reports, checking the data. If one engineer with a good tool does what three did, utilities hire fewer of us. My pass degree makes me nervous about being in the cut, even though my grid field is slower to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and put in extra hours on the real systems side: protection relays, substations, field commissioning. I'd learn the tools properly, maybe a short course in machine learning for forecasting. I'd also join the graduates' section of the engineers' union and see if they bargain over intake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job feels okay, but the whole entry rung is wobbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own work would the software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write the first draft of the load-flow report with the tool, then check every number against a hand calculation. If it's wrong twice in a row on something simple, I stop using it for that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide when to trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd trust it for drafts and not for sign-off. My lecturer Professor Adeyemi says a wrong protection setting can black out a town, and that stuck with me.

Firms shouldn't cut graduate intake **without telling anyone**.
think: Graduate tasks like **load-flow scripts** and reports go first, so utilities hire fewer of us.
My pass degree makes me **nervous** about being in the cut.
do: Do extra hours on **protection relays** and field commissioning.
Take a short **machine learning** course and join the graduates' union section.
feel: Uneasy: my own job feels okay but the **entry rung** is wobbling.

fieldNote: Nervous about being the pass-degree graduate in a **smaller intake**, but picks field skills that software can't do.

steps.text: Take a short machine learning course for grid forecasting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a safety net right now: income support, public retraining, maybe a shorter work week. I'd go on a march with my union. I'd also admit online that I don't have an answer, and that nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be scared for Mum and Dad too. Dad's bus could be driverless by 2031, and Mum's hospital admin side could shrink. My own work, the thinking side of grid planning, could be gone by 2028, right when I graduate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and look for work on the physical side: substations, line crews, commissioning, things that need hands for three more years. I'd move money from savings into a safer account and hold off on anything big. I'd go to every public meeting about support and write to my representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can still plan, but my stomach turns when I think about Dad's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say when you told them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd say we've been through hard times before, and Mum would say we'll manage. Dad would go quiet and then ask whether the bus company will offer him a different job. I'd feel like the one explaining the end of my father's career to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my sister Noor and my parents and go through the family budget line by line. Then I'd email twenty grid contractors about site roles. I'd do those two things before anything else, because they're things I can control.

I'd admit online that I don't have an answer, and **nobody does**.
think: I'm scared for my parents: Dad's bus could be **driverless** by 2031.

Go through the **family budget** line by line with my parents.
feel: Anxious, and my stomach turns when I think about **Dad's job**.
S2.quote: I'd feel like the one explaining the end of my father's career to him.

steps.text: Email twenty grid contractors about substation and site roles

Write to my representative and join the union march

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's enough to act if we move now. I'd push for retraining money and a plan for drivers and hospital staff. I'd say that to friends and at the union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a first job for roughly three years before the full thinking AI arrives. I could build real experience in the field, and be someone useful when the robots come around 2034. I'd be uneasy, but not scared, since there's time to switch if my area shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent graduate post at a utility, probably the grid operator in the city, and save a third of my pay. I'd spend evenings on a part-time course in control systems. I'd also help Dad look at what other work he could do, because his bus job is the one in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It sits in the back of my mind like a bill I know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about having five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be running, but with five I can walk fast. I'd get the job, learn the real kit, and stay close to people who do hands-on work. If I'd landed a team with a good senior engineer, I'd have been in good hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your university to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it to offer short courses to graduates for free for a few years after they finish, and to put real field placements into the master's. Right now my programme is all theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get this right. We could change the school system, fund retraining, and plan for what happens to drivers and clerks. I'd say it at work and online and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty calm. By 2036 I'd have nearly a decade of work and could be leading a small team, moving into the planning side of the grid, which will need people who understand it. If a robot does the site work in 2039 I'd probably be supervising the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the graduate job, work my way up, and pay my parents back by buying them a better car. I'd learn the AI tools properly, because I'd have time. I'd also spend a few evenings a year with Dad, planning what he'd do after the buses go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of excitement. A decade feels like a fair run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise in grid planning with storage and solar, which needs people no matter who is thinking. I'd probably take a short stretch abroad, say a year in a Nordic grid company, to see how others do it. That's a long runway luxury I wouldn't have with two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Noor anything different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Noor to enjoy nursing and not to panic. In ten years there will still be people who need caring for, and she'd have time to add skills, like using the tools for patient notes.

I'd say it at work and online and mean it.

By 2039 I might be **supervising robots** on the site work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because my parents' jobs could go before I even have a pay slip. What would help is a safety net that already exists on the day it happens, like retraining money and income support, and employers who tell people early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just add that I'm lucky, and I know it. People with the same degree and a loan face a very different version of all of this.

headlineQuote: I'm lucky, and I know it. People with the same degree and a loan face a very different version of all of this.
portrait: Wei is a **24-year-old** power-systems master's student who lives at home in Marlow and has no debt.
His parents are a ward nurse and a bus driver, so his worries reach beyond his own **career**.
He is progressive and steady: he uses AI **now and then** and double-checks everything it says.
His mood ranges from calm in the mild worlds to **anxious** when AGI arrives in two years.
He copes with a practical plan: field-side grid work, **family budgeting** and union support.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, because his parents' jobs could go before he has a pay slip.
whatWouldHelp: A **safety net** ready on day one, with retraining money, income support and early warning from employers.
